name: Baking soda toothpaste
lead: Baking soda toothpaste is a dentifrice that contains sodium bicarbonate, usually alongside fluoride, marketed for plaque removal, stain removal, and neutralising acid and odour. Sodium bicarbonate is classed as a mild abrasive and appears in many "natural" toothpaste formulations.[1]

Randomised trials funded in the dental-products field have compared baking soda toothpastes with a regular fluoride toothpaste for plaque and gingivitis and have tested a baking soda formula for tooth sensitivity.[2][3] In appearance culture the product is mainly discussed in connection with whitening and fresher breath, although the sources reviewed document mostly oral-health outcomes rather than tooth colour.

Baking soda and peroxide paste recommended by about 1900[1]

paras: Abrasives make up roughly 8 to 20 percent of a typical toothpaste and work by physically removing plaque and surface stain. Sodium bicarbonate is listed among the representative abrasives.[1] Abrasivity is commonly expressed as a relative dentin abrasivity (RDA) value; one encyclopedia account says the ANSI and the American Dental Association regard values below 250 as safe for lifetime use.[1]

A paste of hydrogen peroxide and baking soda was being recommended for use on toothbrushes by around 1900, and Arm & Hammer sold a baking soda tooth powder in the United States until about 2000.[1] Later patents describe baking soda toothpastes and gels containing soluble pyrophosphate salts.[6][7]
A controlled trial of 208 participants tested a baking soda toothpaste delivering calcium, phosphate and fluoride against a control toothpaste for dentinal hypersensitivity.[2]

A six-month, double-blind randomised study of 319 participants compared fluoride toothpastes containing 35 percent and 20 percent baking soda with a fluoride control toothpaste, measuring plaque and gingivitis indices at 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months.[3] A separate three-month randomised study examined plaque and gingivitis with a baking soda toothpaste.[5]

A 1992 study of 22 dentists examined patient compliance with oral hygiene using a fluoride toothpaste with hydrogen peroxide and baking soda.[4] Studies of whether baking soda toothpaste changes tooth colour were not among the sources reviewed.
Encyclopedic sources note that abrasive toothpastes cause a small amount of enamel wear and that excessive use of whitening toothpaste might damage enamel.[1]

timeline.event: A hydrogen peroxide and baking soda paste is recommended for toothbrush use.[1]
A patent is published for baking soda toothpaste with soluble pyrophosphate salts.[6]
Two randomised studies of baking soda toothpaste and gingival health are published.[3][5]

card.summary: Sodium bicarbonate toothpaste sold for plaque, stain and odour control; the research is mostly on gum health, not whitening.
card.note: Abrasive; whitening effects are not established in the studies reviewed.

quick.overview:
Baking soda toothpaste is an ordinary fluoride toothpaste that includes sodium bicarbonate, a mild abrasive. It is sold for plaque removal, surface stain removal and neutralising acid and odour.

Published trials mostly look at plaque, gum inflammation and tooth sensitivity rather than visible whitening, so its appearance benefit rests largely on the general role of abrasives in removing surface stain.
quick.mechanism: Sodium bicarbonate acts as a mild abrasive that helps lift plaque and surface stain mechanically while brushing; manufacturers also describe it as neutralising acids and odours.
quick.risks: Abrasive toothpastes cause a small amount of enamel wear, and excessive use of whitening pastes might damage enamel according to encyclopedic sources. Abrasivity is rated by RDA value, with values under 250 considered acceptable by ANSI and the ADA.
